validated_results.title: Prospective Study of Avocado Consumption and Cancer Risk in U.S. Men and Women.
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort study reporting multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios for avocado intake and incident bladder cancer in men and women.

sample_size.excerpt: This study included data from 45,289 men in the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study (HPFS, 1986–2016) and 67,039 women in the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS, 1986–2014).

effect_size.excerpt: In HPFS, men who consumed one or more weekly servings of avocado had a 15% lower risk of total cancer compared to those who consumed less than one serving per month (95% CI 0.80–0.91). Men who consumed at least one weekly serving of avocado also had significantly decreased risk of colorectal cancer (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.59–0.85), lung cancer (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.57–0.90), and bladder cancer (HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.57–0.90).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Men who consumed at least one weekly serving of avocado also had significantly decreased risk of colorectal cancer (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.59–0.85), lung cancer (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.57–0.90), and bladder cancer (HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.57–0.90).

comparison.excerpt: Participants’ avocado consumption at each time point was collapsed into three categories: <1 serving per month, 1–3 servings per month, and ≥1 serving per week.

design.excerpt: We leveraged data from two cohort studies: Health Professionals Follow-Up Study (HPFS) and Nurses’ Health Study (NHS).

timing.excerpt: Prospective studies on avocado consumption and cancer risk have yet to be conducted.

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Avocado consumption was assessed using validated food frequency questionnaires every four years.
